strengths: PST addresses a meaningful problem in multimodal NLP fairness: gender associations may change when multiple roles are described together. Examining organizational power extends the analysis beyond occupational representation.

The occupational benchmark systematically crosses 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations in both positional orders. Descriptor lists, prompt templates, detailed results, and a code/data link support transparency.

Three human annotators per image and strong reported agreement (Fleiss’ kappa 0.88–0.92) support the reliability of perceived-gender labels. The occupational breakdown provides credible evidence of stereotypical associations in the evaluated DALL-E-3 outputs.
FairCritic offers a practical approach using natural-language feedback without model training. Its reported aggregate score reductions are promising and warrant further investigation.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation exceeds what SS measures. Equation 1 averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposite imbalances to cancel: depicting every occupation as women would yield overall SS = 0. Table 1 illustrates cancellation with single-person scores of 50 and −30 averaging to 10. Even gender-stratified averages can hide differences across occupations. Consequently, neither the supposedly near-unbiased baseline nor FairCritic’s 'near-perfect fairness' is established. Report gender distributions and absolute deviations from parity for individual occupations and power roles.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but omits exact critic prompts, image batch sizes, bias-decision criteria, feedback incorporation, and complete sampling settings. It is also unclear whether final evaluation uses fresh samples independent of those inspected by the critic. These details are necessary to assess the central mitigation result.

The mitigation comparison does not isolate the benefit of adaptive feedback. Table 2 evaluates the occupational intervention on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic over the full set. Comparisons need identical evaluation prompts and comparable generation budgets. A fixed-guidance or no-image-feedback ablation would help establish whether the visual critic contributes beyond additional fairness instructions. One intervention baseline cannot support broad claims about previous prompt-based methods.

Statistical support is weak for occupation-level amplification and mitigation claims. The single-person baseline uses only three images per identity, and no confidence intervals are provided. Figure 6 also compares events with different baselines: under independent balanced gender sampling, the probability that at least one of two subjects matches its stereotype is already 75%, versus 50% for one subject. Thus, the 74.3% headline alone is not evidence of bias; the reported 'both' rate is more informative.

The evaluation does not establish that generated subjects retain the requested occupations, power roles, and positions, particularly after mitigation. Gender annotation at an expected position can mismeasure occupational bias when roles are swapped or omitted. Report instruction-adherence and failure rates before and after FairCritic, and explain how 'Cannot Identify' responses and annotator disagreements affect scoring.

Reporting inconsistencies impede verification. Reconcile the 944 versus 1,952 prompt counts and clearly distinguish constructed prompts from evaluated samples. In Table 1, FairCritic’s organizational-power subgroup scores, 11.40 and −1.96, average to 4.72 rather than the reported 5.09 under equal weighting. Broken figure references also need correction. Together with the measurement and reproducibility gaps, these issues prevent a positive Findings recommendation in the current form.
